question: Can the interpolation peak associated with double descent be explained using elementary linear algebra by isolating a small set of interpretable spectral and residual factors, and do ablations of those factors remove the peak on synthetic and tabular data?

key_findings.claim: The paper is primarily a tutorial synthesis: it promises visual polynomial intuition, an elementary ordinary-least-squares decomposition, tabular demonstrations, factor ablations, and an informal bridge to nonlinear models.
key_findings.evidence: Its stated goal is accessibility without random-matrix or statistical-physics machinery. The only trained models in the reported experiments are polynomial regression and ordinary linear regression; no deep network is trained despite the title's framing as a deep-learning puzzle.

key_findings.claim: The polynomial example gives an intuitive bias-variance account of the two sides of the interpolation threshold.
key_findings.evidence: Legendre-polynomial features are increased from one to 200 for the target y(x)=2x+cos(25x). Below the threshold, extra features reduce approximation bias; near it, the interpolant develops sample-sensitive oscillations and extreme test error; above it, the selected minimum-coefficient-norm interpolant becomes smoother while preserving zero training error.

key_findings.claim: For full-rank ordinary least squares, the underparameterized and overparameterized estimators use complementary left- and right-pseudoinverse formulas.
key_findings.evidence: When N>P, the paper uses beta_hat=(X^T X)^-1 X^T Y. When P>N, it defines the minimum-Euclidean-norm interpolant beta_hat=X^T(XX^T)^-1Y and connects this choice to zero-initialized gradient flow. These formulas are valid only under the corresponding full-column-rank or full-row-rank assumptions.

key_findings.claim: The exact full-rank decomposition expresses residual-induced prediction error as a sum of inverse-singular-value-weighted mode alignments.
key_findings.evidence: Writing Y=X beta_star+E and X=U Sigma V^T yields, for each nonzero singular mode r, a contribution (1/sigma_r)(x_test dot v_r)(u_r dot E). The overparameterized expression additionally contains a projection-bias term because training rows reveal only an N-dimensional subspace of the P-dimensional coefficient vector.

key_findings.claim: The paper identifies three ingredients for its residual-amplification mechanism: small nonzero training singular values, test-feature alignment with the associated right singular directions, and optimal-model residual alignment with the corresponding left singular directions.
key_findings.evidence: A weakly observed direction amplifies coefficient error through 1/sigma_r; a residual component along u_r makes that fitted coefficient wrong; and a test point with a large projection on v_r turns the coefficient error into prediction error. This mode-level description is the paper's clearest reusable contribution.

key_findings.claim: The overparameterized estimator has a separate bias term caused by coefficient directions invisible to the training row space.
key_findings.evidence: The term x_test [X^T(XX^T)^-1X-I] beta_star is absent in the underparameterized full-column-rank case. The paper interprets it as lost information about beta_star in the P-N unobserved directions, while labeling the residual-amplification sum the variance contribution.

key_findings.claim: The claim that the smallest nonzero singular value typically bottoms out at the interpolation threshold is probabilistic, not distribution-free.
key_findings.evidence: The paper invokes the Marchenko-Pastur distribution but replaces it with a geometric story: as independent observations fill successive directions, the last newly occupied direction near N=P is likely to have little variation, while additional observations beyond P strengthen every direction. This requires random-design, scaling, and effective-rank conditions that are not stated as a theorem for the real datasets.

key_findings.claim: Three small tabular regression datasets exhibit a sample-wise interpolation spike under unregularized ordinary least squares.
key_findings.evidence: WHO Life Expectancy, California Housing, and Diabetes plots show test mean squared error rising sharply near N=P and declining on either side; companion plots show the smallest nonzero singular value approaching its minimum there. The text says the datasets were selected for easy accessibility, not drawn from a defined benchmark population.

key_findings.claim: The proposed ablations suppress the observed peak in one synthetic setting and all three tabular datasets.
key_findings.evidence: The authors truncate small training singular values, restrict test features to retained training singular directions, or replace targets by predictions from a full-dataset linear fit so the constructed linear problem has zero residual. Figure 7 visually reports no double-descent peak after each intervention.

key_findings.claim: Random label noise is not necessary for the residual term: model misspecification can create deterministic residuals.
key_findings.evidence: The decomposition defines E relative to the best member of the selected model class, so E can contain systematic nonlinear structure rather than stochastic noise. The autoencoder discussion uses lossy compression as an example where identical inputs and targets still leave model-class residuals.

key_findings.claim: The nonlinear extension is an analogy through fixed feature maps and infinite-width kernel limits, not a derivation for feature-learning deep networks.
key_findings.evidence: Polynomial regression is rewritten as linear regression on Phi_P(X), and some infinite-width limits are discussed as regression on induced features. The remaining neural evidence is an interpretation of a separate shallow-autoencoder observation; there is no finite-width, learned-feature, classification, optimizer, or epoch-wise experiment here.

key_findings.claim: The printed overparameterized derivation contains an invalid matrix inverse, even though its final SVD residual sum can be repaired with the pseudoinverse.
key_findings.evidence: Page 6 correctly begins with x_test X^T(XX^T)^-1E, then replaces it with x_test (X^T X)^-1X^T E. In the stated P>N regime, rank(X^T X) is at most N<P, so that ordinary inverse does not exist. Page 7 repeats the invalid expression before presenting the correct mode sum. The valid object is X^T(XX^T)^-1=V Sigma^+ U^T under full row rank.

anchors.section: First paragraph and final SVD equations

key_findings.claim: Appendix A also prints a dimensionally invalid left-inverse formula and uses inverse notation for a generally rectangular design matrix.
key_findings.evidence: The displayed underparameterized expression is (X^T X)^-1 X, but X is N by P, so the product of a P by P matrix with an N by P matrix is undefined unless N=P; the correct left pseudoinverse is (X^T X)^-1 X^T. The middle symbol X^-1 is likewise not an ordinary inverse away from the square case.

anchors.section: Appendix A, left inverse / inverse / right inverse display

key_findings.claim: The blanket interpolation statement needs rank and target-compatibility qualifications.
key_findings.evidence: The paper says P at least N permits perfect interpolation, but arbitrary Y is interpolable only when X has full row rank (or Y lies in its column space). Duplicate or collinear rows, categorical encodings, centered designs, and other rank deficiencies break the claim and make the displayed ordinary inverses unavailable; a pseudoinverse formulation would cover these cases.

anchors.section: Definitions of parameterization and interpolation threshold

key_findings.claim: The three factors are not proved to be universally necessary or sufficient for double descent.
key_findings.evidence: The exact residual contribution is a signed sum across modes: nonzero or individually large factors can cancel, and their presence at one sample size does not define a non-monotonic generalization curve. The separate bias term, changing model families, optimization, loss geometry, learned features, and multiple randomness sources can also shape peaks. The paper provides illustrations and interventions but no theorem over a specified sequence of data-generating problems.

anchors.section: Claim that factors create double descent

key_findings.claim: The ablations demonstrate controllability of these examples but do not isolate causal necessity while holding the learning problem fixed.
key_findings.evidence: Singular-value truncation changes the estimator and representation, test projection changes the evaluation covariates, and target replacement changes the task and its test labels. Each intervention can also alter other alignments, bias, effective dimension, and scale, so disappearance of the peak is consistent with the mechanism but is not a controlled causal proof that only the named factor changed.

key_findings.claim: The ridge-regression explanation is spectrally imprecise, and the reported truncation ablation is not ridge regression.
key_findings.evidence: The paper says ridge effectively adds a gap separating the smallest nonzero singular value of X from zero. Ridge does not change X or its singular values; it replaces the pseudoinverse factor 1/sigma with the bounded filter sigma/(sigma^2+lambda), equivalently shifting eigenvalues of X^T X by lambda. The experiment instead deletes singular modes below a cutoff, which is truncated-SVD or principal-component regression.

anchors.section: Section 6, first absent-factor explanation and ablation 1

key_findings.claim: The empirical evidence is visually striking but underreported for a reproducible general claim.
key_findings.evidence: The paper does not specify preprocessing, missing-value handling, feature scaling, intercept treatment, train/test sizes, seeds, exact sampling protocol, uncertainty definition, numerical solver tolerance, or quantitative peak and ablation summaries in the text or tables. The datasets are few and low-dimensional, and results are shown only as plots; the code is linked but no execution audit is part of the paper.

key_findings.claim: The mechanism is parameterization-sensitive, which limits an unqualified interpretation in terms of raw parameter count.
key_findings.evidence: Minimum Euclidean coefficient norm, singular values, and mode alignments change under feature rescaling or a non-orthogonal basis change even when the function class is unchanged. The polynomial result fixes a Legendre basis, and the real-data result fixes the supplied coordinates. No invariant effective-complexity or whitening analysis is given.

method.core_idea: Expose ordinary least-squares prediction error in the singular-vector basis so the interpolation spike can be understood as amplification of residual error along weakly observed directions that matter at test time.
method.mechanism: Fit classical least squares below the threshold and the minimum-norm interpolant above it; write targets as an ideal linear component plus residuals; decompose the design matrix with an SVD; identify the inverse singular value, test/right-singular alignment, and residual/left-singular alignment in every error mode; then intervene on each factor and resweep sample size.
assumptions: The underparameterized design has full column rank and the overparameterized design has full row rank.
Unregularized squared-error linear regression and its minimum-Euclidean-norm interpolant are the relevant learning rules.
Zero-initialized gradient flow or a compatible solver selects the Moore-Penrose solution in the overparameterized regime.
A fixed feature coordinate system and coefficient norm are meaningful for interpreting singular directions.
The test target can be compared to x_test dot beta_star, with residual effects analyzed separately from the overparameterized projection bias.
Random-design intuition akin to Marchenko-Pastur behavior makes a very small nonzero singular value likely near N=P.
The chosen tabular datasets, preprocessing, and sample-size sweeps preserve the mechanism the tutorial aims to isolate.
Fixed-feature or kernel-limit intuition is informative about nonlinear finite-width neural networks.

techniques.role: Makes the interpolation peak and minimum-norm second descent visually accessible in one dimension.
Selects a unique interpolating solution in the underdetermined linear system.
Separates inverse spectral amplification, test-direction alignment, and residual-direction alignment mode by mode.
Moves a fixed-dimensional linear problem through the overparameterized, interpolation, and underparameterized regimes.
Removes weakly observed directions as the first mechanism ablation.
Suppresses evaluation variation in selected trailing training-feature directions.
Constructs zero model-class residuals by replacing labels with a full-data linear fit.
Relates the linear calculation to polynomial features and some infinite-width neural limits.

evaluations.setting: One-dimensional Legendre-polynomial regression with target y(x)=2x+cos(25x) and feature count swept from 1 to 200
evaluations.metric: Train and test mean squared error plus fitted-curve visualizations
evaluations.result: A many-orders-of-magnitude test-error peak appears near interpolation and declines for larger minimum-norm models
evaluations.baseline: The same polynomial family on the underparameterized and overparameterized sides; no ridge or alternative basis

evaluations.setting: Ordinary linear regression on WHO Life Expectancy, California Housing, and Diabetes while varying the number of training samples
evaluations.metric: Test mean squared error and smallest nonzero training-design singular value
evaluations.result: All three plots show a sharp error peak and a singular-value minimum near N=P

evaluations.setting: Student-teacher synthetic data and the same three real datasets
evaluations.metric: Visual disappearance of the test-error peak after each proposed ablation
evaluations.result: Truncating small singular values, projecting test features, or constructing zero-residual targets suppresses the displayed peak in every row of Figure 7
evaluations.baseline: Unablated ordinary least squares on each dataset

limitations: Two printed overparameterized steps invoke (X^T X)^-1 where that inverse cannot exist, and Appendix A contains a separate dimensionally invalid left-inverse formula.
Full row or column rank is assumed implicitly; rank-deficient designs and non-interpolable labels require a pseudoinverse treatment.
The three factors exactly describe one residual-amplification term, not a proved universal necessary-and-sufficient characterization of every double-descent curve.
Signed contributions can cancel across singular modes, and the overparameterized bias term is not incorporated into the three-factor claim.
The near-threshold singular-value argument relies on unstated random-design and effective-rank conditions rather than holding for arbitrary data.
The ablations change the estimator, covariates, or target task and therefore do not hold all other causal factors fixed.
The text conflates ridge's spectral shrinkage with changing X's singular values, while the implemented hard cutoff is a different estimator.
Feature scaling and basis changes alter minimum norm, spectra, and alignments, so the explanation is not invariant to equivalent parameterizations.
Only three small tabular datasets and one synthetic setup are evaluated, with crucial preprocessing and uncertainty details absent from the paper.
No quantitative effect sizes, peak-location errors, confidence intervals, solver-stability checks, or comparison to theoretical risk formulas are reported.
No deep network is trained; finite-width feature learning, classification losses, optimizer dynamics, and epoch-wise double descent are outside the evidence.
In ordinary linear regression the number of parameters equals feature dimension, whereas those quantities are decoupled in deep networks.
Calling the pointwise residual sum variance is informal without an expectation over a specified source of randomness.
The code is advertised but the manuscript is not self-contained enough to reproduce the figures from its methods description alone.
failure_modes: Duplicate or collinear training rows make XX^T singular, so the claimed overparameterized formula and arbitrary-label interpolation fail.
Correlated or low-effective-rank data place the smallest nonzero singular value far from N=P or generate several spectral transitions.
Two large singular-mode contributions have opposite signs and cancel for a test point despite all three named factors being large.
A feature rescaling moves the minimum-norm solution and the apparent peak without changing the represented function class.
Finite-precision inversion near N=P creates a numerical blow-up that is mistaken for population-risk divergence.
A ridge penalty, early stopping, solver tolerance, or nonzero initialization selects a different solution and changes or removes the curve.
Learned neural features rotate and rescale during training, so a fixed input-design SVD does not track the operative directions.
Train and test covariances differ, making test-direction alignment reflect distribution shift rather than the tutorial's iid mechanism.
A peak caused by changing which kinds of parameters are added is misattributed solely to crossing the interpolation threshold.
An underparameterized or multiple-descent peak arises from structured spectra and target alignment outside the tutorial's generic threshold story.
The zero-residual ablation leaks full-dataset information through beta_star and turns the original prediction task into an easier constructed one.
reusable_insights: Inspect error in singular modes: weak training directions are dangerous only when residuals contaminate them and test points use them.
Distinguish stochastic label noise from residual error relative to the selected model class; misspecification alone can drive interpolation instability.
State the optimizer's implicit norm because overparameterized predictions depend on which interpolant is selected.
Use a pseudoinverse from the beginning to make linear derivations correct across both rank regimes.
Report spectra together with target and test alignments; condition number alone cannot determine generalization error.
Stress-test double-descent claims under feature rescaling, whitening, alternate bases, ridge, and multiple solvers.
Ablations are strongest when they preserve the data-generating task and verify that non-target factors remain unchanged.
Separate sample-wise, parameter-wise, and epoch-wise curves rather than treating their horizontal axes as interchangeable.
For learned models, track representation spectra, residual alignments, and test alignments throughout training rather than only at the input layer.
open_questions: Under what explicit distributional and scaling assumptions are the three mode factors necessary or sufficient for a population-risk peak?
Can a corrected pseudoinverse derivation cover rank deficiency, intercepts, centered features, repeated singular values, and multi-output regression cleanly?
How often do cross-mode cancellations materially weaken predictions based on the smallest singular value alone?
Which coordinate-invariant effective-complexity or spectral quantities predict a peak across equivalent feature parameterizations?
Can interventions remove one alignment factor while preserving the target function, test distribution, other alignments, and bias term?
How does feature learning in finite-width neural networks change singular values and residual alignments around model-wise and epoch-wise interpolation?
What quantitative relation between finite-sample condition number, numerical precision, and population test risk separates computational from statistical divergence?
When do optimal ridge, early stopping, ensembling, or alternative implicit norms eliminate versus merely shift a peak?
How should the framework change for classification, cross-entropy, non-interpolable data, and non-iid test distributions?
Can one unified experiment compare the residual-mode account, fine-grained bias-variance, Hessian-spectrum, effective-parameter, and generalized-aliasing explanations?
What prospective benchmark across many datasets predicts peak location and magnitude before observing test labels?

competitive_landscape.title: Reconciling Modern Machine Learning Practice and the Bias-Variance Trade-off
competitive_landscape.relationship: Introduced and popularized the unified double-descent curve across model families and datasets.
competitive_landscape.difference: Belkin et al. establish the broad empirical framing and posit a mechanism; Schaeffer et al. narrow to an elementary singular-mode explanation and targeted ablations for ordinary regression.

competitive_landscape.title: Surprises in High-Dimensional Ridgeless Least Squares Interpolation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Derives rigorous asymptotic and non-asymptotic risk results for minimum-norm linear and random-feature regression.
competitive_landscape.difference: It gives quantitatively precise double-descent conditions under explicit random-design assumptions; the target trades that rigor for a shorter pointwise SVD tutorial and small real-data demonstrations.

competitive_landscape.title: Benign Overfitting in Linear Regression
competitive_landscape.relationship: Characterizes covariance effective-rank conditions under which a minimum-norm interpolator has near-optimal prediction accuracy.
competitive_landscape.difference: Bartlett et al. explain when the far-overparameterized regime is benign; the target focuses on why residual error can blow up near interpolation and does not characterize eventual risk.

competitive_landscape.title: The Generalization Error of Random Features Regression: Precise Asymptotics and Double Descent Curve
competitive_landscape.relationship: Computes high-dimensional test-risk asymptotics for ridge regression on random nonlinear features, including the full double-descent curve.
competitive_landscape.difference: It supplies an analytically tractable nonlinear-feature model and joint width/sample/dimension limit; Schaeffer et al. only analogize fixed features to nonlinear networks and run no neural experiment.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v5; Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 75(4), 2022

competitive_landscape.title: Double Descent in the Condition Number
competitive_landscape.relationship: Shows that random rectangular linear systems are typically worst conditioned near the square interpolation point.
competitive_landscape.difference: This is the closest spectral precursor to the target's inverse-smallest-singular-value intuition; the target adds residual and test-vector alignments, correctly showing why conditioning alone is not prediction error.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Double Descent: Where Bigger Models and More Data Hurt
competitive_landscape.relationship: Demonstrates model-wise, epoch-wise, and sample-wise double descent in modern deep-learning tasks and proposes effective model complexity.
competitive_landscape.difference: It provides the finite-network phenomenon the target seeks to make intuitive; the target analyzes only sample-wise linear regression and does not validate its mechanism for model- or epoch-wise neural curves.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v1; Journal of Statistical Mechanics 2021(12)

competitive_landscape.title: Optimal Regularization Can Mitigate Double Descent
competitive_landscape.relationship: Proves monotonic sample- and model-size risk for optimally tuned ridge in specific isotropic linear models and demonstrates mitigation in neural networks.
competitive_landscape.difference: It studies a practical regularization protocol and its assumptions; the target uses hard singular-value deletion as an explanatory ablation and does not evaluate tuned ridge.

competitive_landscape.title: Multiple Descent: Design Your Own Generalization Curve
competitive_landscape.relationship: Constructs linear-regression families with arbitrarily many controllable generalization peaks.
competitive_landscape.difference: It proves that curve shape is an interaction of data and inductive bias rather than an intrinsic two-descent law, limiting any universal reading of the target's generic three-factor threshold story.

competitive_landscape.title: Memorizing without Overfitting: Bias, Variance, and Interpolation in Over-parameterized Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: A same-coauthor predecessor derives analytic bias and variance in linear and nonlinear two-layer models, including no-label-noise overfitting.
competitive_landscape.difference: It is mathematically broader and already establishes variance divergence and nonlinear cases; the target's novelty is its elementary mode-wise pedagogy and visual ablation panel rather than the underlying phenomenon.

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Double Descent Requires a Fine-Grained Bias-Variance Decomposition
competitive_landscape.relationship: Decomposes variance by sampling, initialization, and label randomness and finds interpolation divergence without label noise in random-feature kernel regression.
competitive_landscape.difference: Adlam and Pennington expose interactions among randomness sources that the target's single fixed-design residual sum does not separate; they also derive asymptotic curves and ensemble/bagging predictions.

competitive_landscape.title: The Geometry of Over-parameterized Regression and Adversarial Perturbations
competitive_landscape.relationship: Develops a feature-space geometry for under- and overparameterized regression and explains double descent with and without label noise.
competitive_landscape.difference: It provides geometric and bias-variance analyses across linear and nonlinear basis models; the target reorganizes a related view into three directly ablated singular-mode factors.

competitive_landscape.title: Phenomenology of Double Descent in Finite-Width Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Analyzes finite-width neural networks through influence functions and Hessian spectra, including the effect of the loss function.
competitive_landscape.difference: It directly targets the nonlinear finite-width and loss-dependent gap left by linear/kernel explanations; Schaeffer et al.'s deep-network extension remains an informal fixed-feature analogy.

competitive_landscape.title: Least Squares Regression Can Exhibit Under-Parameterized Double Descent
competitive_landscape.relationship: A near-concurrent/later work constructs and proves least-squares peaks strictly inside the underparameterized regime through spectrum and target-eigenvector alignment.
competitive_landscape.difference: Its counterexamples show that peaks need not sit at interpolation and that prevailing threshold explanations are incomplete, sharpening the limits of the target's Marchenko-Pastur-centered intuition.

competitive_landscape.title: A U-turn on Double Descent: Rethinking Parameter Counting in Statistical Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: A later critique shows that apparent second descents in several classical models coincide with switching between different parameter-growth mechanisms rather than inherently with p=n.
competitive_landscape.difference: It replaces raw parameter count with a test-aware effective-parameter view and can fold curves back into classical shapes; the target treats N/P and the interpolation threshold as the main organizing axis.

competitive_landscape.title: eGAD! Double Descent Is Explained by Generalized Aliasing Decomposition
competitive_landscape.relationship: A later decomposition separates model insufficiency, data insufficiency, and generalized aliasing across random features, signal processing, differential equations, and materials prediction.
competitive_landscape.difference: GAD is designed to explain double and multiple descents across broader linear-function settings and can inform design without labels; the target isolates label/residual amplification in OLS and three small datasets.

competitive_landscape.title: Unified Neural Network Scaling Laws and Scale-time Equivalence
competitive_landscape.relationship: A same-author later work combines a linear double-descent analysis with scale-time equivalence and tests a joint size, training-time, and data-volume law on vision networks.
competitive_landscape.difference: It begins to connect the target's linear intuition to finite neural architectures and multiple scaling axes, although its broader scaling claims require separate validation and are not evidence retroactively contained in the tutorial.

competitive_landscape.title: Exact Expressions for Double Descent and Implicit Regularization via Surrogate Random Design
competitive_landscape.relationship: Derives exact non-asymptotic mean-squared-error expressions for minimum-norm linear estimation under a surrogate random design and connects overparameterization to implicit ridge regularization.
competitive_landscape.difference: It predates the target and is theoretically sharper about expected risk and implicit regularization, while the target is more elementary and per-test-point but supplies no comparable risk theorem.

competitive_landscape.title: Spectrum Dependent Learning Curves in Kernel Regression and Wide Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Decomposes population generalization by kernel eigenmodes and analyzes the successive learning of spectral components in kernel regression and wide networks.
competitive_landscape.difference: Its eigenmode learning curves operate at the distribution/kernel level; the target uses an empirical design SVD and one test point's projections without deriving an expected learning curve.

competitive_landscape.title: Double Trouble in Double Descent: Bias and Variance(s) in the Lazy Regime
competitive_landscape.relationship: Separates sampling, label, and initialization variance in lazy/random-feature models and analyzes how averaging changes the interpolation peak.
competitive_landscape.difference: It provides causal attribution among distinct randomness sources; the target compresses all unfit structure into u_r dot E, gaining simplicity while losing that source-level resolution.

competitive_landscape.title: Triple Descent and the Two Kinds of Overfitting: Where & Why Do They Appear?
competitive_landscape.relationship: Distinguishes nonlinear/random-feature and linear/noise interpolation transitions and shows that two peaks can coexist as triple descent.
competitive_landscape.difference: It demonstrates that visually similar peaks can occur at different effective transitions and respond differently to noise and regularization, limiting a single universal three-factor narrative.

competitive_landscape.title: Early Stopping in Deep Networks: Double Descent and How to Eliminate It
competitive_landscape.relationship: Explains epoch-wise double descent through components learned at different rates and shows how layerwise step-size control can remove it.
competitive_landscape.difference: That is an optimization-dynamical mechanism for finite deep networks, entirely outside the target's converged static OLS factorization.

competitive_landscape.title: Post-Hoc Reversal: Are We Selecting Models Prematurely?
competitive_landscape.relationship: A later study that cites the target shows post-hoc temperature scaling can induce double descent while ensembling and stochastic weight averaging can flatten it.
competitive_landscape.difference: It demonstrates that the observed curve depends on metric and post-hoc prediction transformation, variables absent from the target's raw squared-error OLS account.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first approachable treatment that combines polynomial visualization, elementary ordinary-linear-regression analysis, real-data evidence, direct ablation of three interpretable causes, and insights for nonlinear networks.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper provides a compact SVD decomposition and a four-by-four visual ablation grid, but spectral conditioning, ridgeless-risk divergence, benign overfitting, residual/noise-free peaks, fine-grained bias-variance, multiple descents, and finite-network mechanisms all have substantial predecessors. Its mathematical scope is full-rank unregularized OLS, and the printed proof contains two inverse errors.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The durable novelty is pedagogical and diagnostic: the product of inverse singular scale, test alignment, and residual alignment is a memorable way to inspect one concrete interpolation-instability mechanism, and the three intervention families make that mechanism visually testable. It does not demystify double descent universally, establish necessary-and-sufficient conditions, or empirically explain deep learning. Correcting the pseudoinverse algebra and narrowing the claim to residual-driven OLS divergence would make the contribution substantially sounder.

reviewer_notes: Read all 15 extracted pages, including the full derivation, every figure, references, and implicit-regularization appendix; visually checked pages 3, 5, 6, 7, 11, and 15 to distinguish extraction artifacts from printed equations. The two invalid inverse displays are present in the PDF itself, while the final SVD residual sum is recoverable with the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. A parallel primary-source search found no dedicated paper-level correction or rebuttal of arxiv:2303.14151; later papers mainly constrain its generality. Competitor records were checked through 2026-08-23. The linked code was not executed, so reproducibility judgments here concern what the manuscript itself specifies.
